sections.h2: Who sets and collects property tax in Virginia?
sections.html:
Virginia real estate tax is local. The state does not bill a house; your county, city or town does, and rates, due dates and many relief programs vary by locality. Virginia is divided into 95 counties and 38 independent cities, which the Census Bureau treats as county equivalents, and the differences between a county and a city are small and relate to how each assesses new taxes, bond referendums and Dillon's Rule (Wikipedia, Virginia).

Two local officers matter most. The commissioner of the revenue, or an equivalent assessing officer, sets the value and handles corrections. The treasurer, or an equivalent officer, collects the bill and runs delinquent tax enforcement. Both offices are listed on your locality's website, and the treasurer can give you a payoff figure for a closing.

sections.h2: How is a Virginia house valued for tax?
sections.html:
All real estate is taxable unless the law exempts it, and general reassessments and annual assessments are made at 100 percent of fair market value (Va. Code 58.1-3201). A tax bill therefore tracks the locality's estimate of what the house would sell for, not what you paid.

How often that estimate changes depends on where you live. Counties must reassess every four years, or every three if the board of supervisors votes for it. A county with a population of 50,000 or less may choose five or six year intervals, and Augusta and Bedford counties have the same option (Va. Code 58.1-3252). A county or city with a qualified full-time appraiser may instead adopt biennial or annual assessment by ordinance, in which case real estate is assessed as of January 1 each year (Va. Code 58.1-3253).

sections.h2: When is Virginia property tax due, and what are the penalties?
sections.html:
Each locality sets its own due dates. A governing body may require payment in a single installment or in two equal installments, and it sets penalties and interest by ordinance (Va. Code 58.1-3916). Check the treasurer's calendar for your address, because two neighboring localities can bill on different schedules.

The state caps what a locality can add. Interest may start the day after the due date at no more than 10 percent a year, with a higher ceiling for the second and later years of delinquency. A late payment penalty cannot exceed 10 percent of the tax past due, or $10 if that is greater, and never more than the tax itself. A locality may also recover collection or attorney fees actually contracted for, up to 20 percent of the delinquent taxes.

Some relief exists in the same statute:

  • A locality may grant a payment extension of up to 90 days for good cause.
  • Members of the armed forces deployed outside the United States get an automatic extension on real estate tax on a primary residence, ending 90 days after deployment.
  • No penalty applies when a late assessment was the fault of a local official and is paid within two weeks of the notice.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Virginia property assessment?
sections.html:
Start with the assessor's office, then the local board of equalization, then the circuit court. The board hears complaints, can raise as well as lower assessments, and works from a presumption that the assessor's value is correct. To win, the owner must show by a preponderance of the evidence that the property is valued above fair market value, or that the assessment is not uniform and was not done under accepted appraisal practice (Va. Code 58.1-3379).

Market sales through December 31 before the assessment's effective date can be used, if the owner submits them by the locality's application deadline. For a home with fewer than four residential units, the assessor must provide written notice and, on written request, the assessment records within 15 days.

Two other paths exist:

  • Application to the commissioner of the revenue for correction, within three years of the end of the tax year or one year from assessment, whichever is later. For real estate, this reaches errors made by the commissioner or factual errors in a general reassessment (Va. Code 58.1-3980).
  • Application to the circuit court, within three years from the last day of the tax year, or one year from assessment or the final determination of an earlier step, whichever is later. For real estate, the court starts from the same presumption that the assessor's value is correct (Va. Code 58.1-3984).

A bill is not treated as delinquent while an administrative appeal is pending, as long as the appeal was filed within 90 days of the assessment, and for 30 days after the final decision.

sections.h2: Are there exemptions or deferrals for older owners?
sections.html:
Possibly, but only if your locality has adopted them. A county, city or town may by ordinance exempt or defer real estate tax for owners who are at least 65, or permanently and totally disabled if the ordinance says so, and who occupy the property as their sole dwelling (Va. Code 58.1-3210).

The ordinance can limit relief to the increase in tax since the owner reached 65 or became disabled. A home held by a life estate, a revocable trust the owner controls, or certain irrevocable trusts can qualify, but a leasehold interest cannot. Ask your commissioner of the revenue about income and net worth limits, because those are set locally and differ from place to place.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid property tax when a Virginia house sells?
sections.html:
The tax has to be paid from the sale. Real estate taxes are a lien ahead of every other lien until the taxing authority is actually paid, and the buyer, or the trustee at a foreclosure sale, must see that proceeds go to taxes and levies assessed on the property (Va. Code 58.1-3340). Taxes and levies there include accrued penalty and interest. The lien also reaches rents for the current year.

For a partial sale of a larger tract, the proration follows the purchase price in relation to the assessed value of the whole tract. The seller's liability is prorated in the contract.

Timing at the closing table adds a wrinkle. If ownership changes after January 1 and the bill has already gone out, the treasurer may cancel the bill sent to the prior owner and reissue it to the new owner, and no penalty applies if the new bill is paid within two weeks of notice.

sections.h2: What if the taxes are years behind?
sections.html:
The locality can sue to sell the property. Real estate with taxes delinquent on December 31 after the second anniversary of the due date can be sold, and the clock is one year for property with a condemned structure, a nuisance, a derelict building or a blighted designation. Property assessed at $100,000 or less can be sold on a court finding of delinquency after the first anniversary (Va. Code 58.1-3965).

Before suing, the collecting officer must send notice at least 30 days ahead to the owner's address on file and to the property address, and publish the list in a local newspaper. The owner can redeem any time before the sale by paying everything owed. Partial payment does not stop the case. The treasurer may suspend the sale under an installment agreement of up to 72 months, which must also keep current taxes paid.

If a property is sold, the former owner and heirs are entitled to the surplus after taxes, penalties, interest, fees, costs and liens, but must claim it within two years of confirmation or it goes to the locality (Va. Code 58.1-3967).

sections.h2: What do taxes mean for a quick sale of a Virginia house?
sections.html:
They mean the payoff figure matters more than the headline price. Before agreeing to any offer, request a current tax statement from the treasurer and ask the title company to list every lien. Add the state recordation tax of 25 cents per $100 and the seller's grantor tax of 50 cents per $500, unless the contract shifts it (Va. Code 58.1-802).

Owners with a pending assessment appeal, a deferral under a local ordinance or an installment agreement should tell the buyer's title company early, since each of these can affect what is owed at closing.

faqs.q: Who do I call about my Virginia property tax bill?
faqs.a: Your locality's treasurer collects the bill, and the commissioner of the revenue or equivalent assessing office sets the value. Both are county, city or town offices, not state offices.

faqs.q: How often is my house reassessed?
faqs.a: In a county, at least every four years, or three if the board of supervisors votes for it, with five or six year options for counties of 50,000 people or fewer. A county or city with a qualified appraiser may assess annually or every two years.

faqs.q: What is the highest penalty a locality may charge for late real estate tax?
faqs.a: A penalty may not exceed 10 percent of the tax past due, or $10 if greater, and never more than the tax itself. Interest may not exceed 10 percent a year, with a higher ceiling in the second and later years.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house while a tax appeal is open?
faqs.a: Yes. The unpaid tax is still a lien, so expect the title company to pay it from proceeds. Tell them about the appeal so the payoff is figured correctly.

faqs.q: Does Virginia have a senior property tax break?
faqs.a: Only where the locality has adopted one. A county, city or town may exempt or defer tax for owners age 65 or older, or disabled if the ordinance allows, on a sole dwelling.

faqs.q: How long do I have to pay before a house can be sold for taxes?
faqs.a: Delinquency on December 31 after the second anniversary of the due date is the usual trigger. It is one year for condemned, nuisance, derelict or blighted property, and for property assessed at $100,000 or less on a court finding.
